description: The Five Pillars, Ten Obligatory Acts, Salah, wudu, du'a and the Shahadah explained.
content_html:
Islam as a Way of Life

Islam is not simply a set of beliefs — it is a complete way of life. The Arabic word islam itself means ‘submission’ or ‘surrender’. For Muslims, every action — eating, working, praying, giving — is an act of worship when carried out with the right intention (niyyah). This holistic understanding means that the rituals Muslims perform are not separate from daily life but are woven into it.

The Five Pillars of Sunni Islam

Sunni Muslims structure their faith around the Five Pillars. The analogy of a house and its pillars is often used: just as a house collapses without structural supports, a Muslim’s faith would collapse without these five foundations.

  • Shahadah — the declaration of faith
  • Salat — five daily prayers
  • Zakat — compulsory almsgiving (2.5% of savings)
  • Sawm — fasting during Ramadan
  • Hajj — pilgrimage to Mecca at least once in a lifetime
Key Fact

The Five Pillars are obligatory for every Sunni Muslim who is able to fulfil them. Together they represent the structural framework of Muslim life, combining declaration, prayer, charity, self-discipline and pilgrimage.

The Ten Obligatory Acts of Shi’a Islam

Shi’a Muslims organise their practice around the Ten Obligatory Acts (known in Arabic as the ‘Furu’ ad-Din’, or branches of the faith). These go beyond the Five Pillars and include additional duties specific to Shi’a practice:

  1. Salat — five daily prayers
  2. Sawm — fasting
  3. Zakat — charitable giving
  4. Khums — a twenty percent tax on certain earnings, paid to the Imam or his representatives
  5. Hajj — pilgrimage to Mecca
  6. Jihad — striving in the way of Allah (see below)
  7. Amr-bil-Maroof — commanding what is right
  8. Nahi Anil Munkar — forbidding what is wrong
  9. Tawalla — expressing love for the friends of Allah (the Imams and their followers)
  10. Tabarra — expressing disassociation from the enemies of Allah

Both traditions share the same core practices — prayer, fasting, almsgiving and pilgrimage. The Shi’a Ten Obligatory Acts extend this framework to include Khums (a second form of financial giving), Jihad as a religious duty, and the paired obligations of Amr-bil-Maroof and Nahi Anil Munkar (promoting good and forbidding evil). Tawalla and Tabarra reflect Shi’a loyalty to the Imams and theological boundaries. A common misconception is that the Shi’a reject the Five Pillars — in fact they perform the same core acts but within a broader obligatory framework. Examiners often ask students to compare these two structures, so knowing all ten acts by name is essential.

The Shahadah

The Shahadah is the declaration: la ilaha illa-llah, muhammadur-rasulu-llah — “There is no god but Allah, and Muhammad is the messenger of Allah.” It is unique among the Five Pillars because it is the only one that is not an action. Saying the Shahadah with sincerity is itself an act of worship.

The Shahadah punctuates the key moments of a Muslim’s life. It is whispered as the first words into the ear of a newborn baby. It is recited at the moment of conversion to Islam. It is said at, or to, a person who is dying. Tawhid — the absolute oneness of Allah — is the theological heart of the Shahadah: there is no partner, equal or associate to Allah.

Key Fact

The Shahadah — la ilaha illa-llah, muhammadur-rasulu-llah — is said at birth, conversion and death. It is the only ‘non-action’ pillar: speaking it sincerely is itself an act of submission to Allah, confirming belief in Tawhid.

Salah: Five Daily Prayers

Salah is direct communication with Allah. The Qur’an instructs: “Maintain with care the [obligatory] prayers and [in particular] the middle prayer and stand before Allah, devoutly obedient” (Surah 2:238, al-Baqarah). Muslims pray five times a day: Fajr (before dawn), Zuhr (midday), Asr (afternoon), Maghrib (after sunset) and Isha (night).

Before prayer, Muslims must perform wudu (ritual ablution). The worshipper washes the face, hands and arms to the elbow, wipes the head and washes the feet. This physical purification represents spiritual readiness to stand before Allah. The direction of prayer — facing Mecca — is called the qibla. Each unit of prayer is called a raka’t. Different prayers have different numbers of raka’t.

Jummah is the Friday midday prayer, which replaces Zuhr and is obligatory for adult Muslim men. The Qur’an says: “O you who have believed, when [the adhan] is called for the prayer on the day of Jumu’ah [Friday], then proceed to the remembrance of Allah” (Surah 62:9, al-Jumuah). The prayer is preceded by the khutba — a sermon given by the imam covering both religious and community matters. Women are permitted but not required to attend Jummah. In Muslim-majority countries, businesses often close at midday on Fridays to allow attendance.

Du’a: Personal Supplication

Du’a is private, personal prayer. Unlike Salah, which follows a fixed set of Arabic recitations in specific body positions at set times, du’a can be spoken in any language, at any time and in any posture. It is the Muslim speaking directly and intimately to Allah from the heart. The Qur’an promises: “And when My servants ask you concerning Me — indeed I am near. I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me” (Surah 2:186, al-Baqarah). Du’a is used to express gratitude, seek forgiveness, ask for guidance and pray for others. It reflects the deeply personal dimension of a Muslim’s relationship with Allah, beyond the structure of formal worship.
exam_tip_html: When using the command word ‘Outline’, give a clear description without extended analysis. When using ‘Explain’, you must show understanding of significance, not just list facts. A very common exam error on this topic is confusing Sunni and Shi’a practice: the Five Pillars belong to Sunni Islam; the Ten Obligatory Acts to Shi’a. Make sure you name them correctly and never credit Sunni Muslims with performing Khums (that is Shi’a only). For the 15-mark Discuss question, develop both sides and reach a justified conclusion, mentioning sources of authority such as Surah 2:238 or Surah 2:186. Accurate spelling of technical terms — Shahadah, niyyah, qibla, raka’t, Jummah, Tawhid — is rewarded on extended responses.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Sunni Muslims observe the Five Pillars (Shahadah, Salat, Zakat, Sawm, Hajj); Shi’a Muslims follow the Ten Obligatory Acts, which include Khums, Amr-bil-Maroof, Nahi Anil Munkar, Tawalla and Tabarra in addition to the shared core.
  • Salah involves ritual purity (wudu), facing the qibla, and units of prayer (raka’t); Friday Jummah prayer with the khutba is obligatory for adult Muslim men.
  • Du’a is personal supplication — informal, in any language, at any time — distinct from the structured ritual of Salah; both express total submission to Allah (Tawhid).

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by the term 'Shahadah'.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for: the Islamic declaration of faith / the statement 'There is no god but Allah and Muhammad is the messenger of Allah' / la ilaha illa-llah, muhammadur-rasulu-llah. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what Muslims do when they perform wudu.
practice_questions.marks: Two marks for any two of the following points: washing the face / washing the hands and arms to the elbow / wiping the head / washing the feet / it is ritual purification performed before Salah / the purpose is physical and spiritual cleanliness before standing before Allah. [2 marks — 1 mark per valid point]

practice_questions.text: Outline the difference between Salah and du'a in Islamic worship.
practice_questions.marks: Three marks for: Salah is formal / structured / has a set number of units (raka't) / uses Arabic / performed at five set times / requires wudu and facing the qibla (any two developed). Du'a is personal / informal / can be in any language / at any time / in any posture / is supplication from the heart (any one developed). Award three marks for a clear, developed contrast covering both forms. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which the Five Pillars are important for Sunni Muslims.
Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The Five Pillars unite all Sunni Muslims in shared practice regardless of nationality or culture — performing the same prayers at the same times creates a global community (ummah). Surah 2:238 commands Muslims to maintain prayers carefully, showing these are divine obligations.
• The Five Pillars structure daily life around submission to Allah, reinforcing Tawhid — the belief in Allah's absolute oneness. Each pillar is an act of obedience that strengthens faith and reminds Muslims of their purpose.
• Salat, performed five times daily, provides regular direct communication with Allah, preventing the believer from becoming spiritually distant.
• The Pillars are described using the analogy of a house and its pillars — without them, a Muslim's faith has no structural support.
Mastering: Two developed points each supported by a named source of wisdom, clear explanation of significance, and coherent expression.
Secure: Two developed points with at least one source of wisdom.
Developing: Two points but limited development or no source.
Emerging: One point, brief or undeveloped. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'The Five Pillars are the most important feature of Muslim life.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• The Five Pillars are obligatory for all Sunni Muslims and cover the full scope of worship — declaration, prayer, giving, fasting and pilgrimage. They are the structural framework ('the pillars of the house') without which faith collapses.
• Salat, five times daily, is the most regular reminder of Allah's presence and keeps Muslims in constant communication with God. Surah 2:238 stresses maintaining prayer with care.
• The Shahadah is the gateway to Islam and encapsulates the core theological belief in Tawhid and the prophethood of Muhammad.
• Without the Pillars being fulfilled, a Muslim cannot be said to be fully practising their faith.

Arguments against / other perspectives:
• Shi'a Muslims follow the Ten Obligatory Acts, which extend beyond the Five Pillars to include Khums, Amr-bil-Maroof, Nahi Anil Munkar, Tawalla and Tabarra. For them, the Five Pillars alone do not cover the full requirement.
• Inner faith and correct belief (niyyah, Tawhid) could be argued to be more fundamental than external ritual practice — without sincere intention, the actions carry no spiritual weight.
• Other features of Muslim life such as the Qur'an, the Sunnah of the Prophet and adherence to Shari'ah law shape moral conduct as much as the Pillars do.
• Du'a — personal, spontaneous prayer — represents the most direct and intimate form of communication with Allah and is practised beyond the structured Pillars.

Mastering: Both sides fully developed with named sources (e.g. Surah 2:238, Surah 2:186), explicit comparison of Sunni and Shi'a practice, explicit weighing, and a justified personal conclusion.
Secure: Both sides developed, at least one source, clear conclusion.
Developing: Some engagement with both sides but limited sources or thin conclusion.
Emerging: One-sided or very brief response with minimal development. [15 marks — SPaG assessed]

practice_questions.text: Outline the Ten Obligatory Acts observed by Shi'a Muslims.
practice_questions.marks: Three marks for a clear, accurate outline identifying at least five of the Ten Obligatory Acts with brief explanation: Salat (prayer), Sawm (fasting), Zakat (almsgiving), Khums (20% tax on earnings), Hajj (pilgrimage), Jihad (striving in the way of Allah), Amr-bil-Maroof (commanding good), Nahi Anil Munkar (forbidding wrong), Tawalla (love for the friends of Allah), Tabarra (disassociation from enemies of Allah). Award three marks for a developed, accurate outline covering distinct acts. [3 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the Five Pillars of Sunni Islam?
What is the meaning of 'du'a' in Islamic worship?
options: The compulsory five daily prayers in Arabic
Personal, informal supplication spoken in any language at any time

knowledge_checks.q: The declaration 'la ilaha illa-llah, muhammadur-rasulu-llah' is known as the _____.
Muslims face the direction of Mecca when praying; this direction is called the _____.
Match each term to its correct meaning:

flashcard_questions.q: What is the collective name for the five obligatory acts of worship in Sunni Islam?

flashcard_questions.a: The Islamic declaration of faith: 'There is no god but Allah and Muhammad is His messenger.'

flashcard_questions.q: The Shahadah is called the only 'non-action' pillar — why?
flashcard_questions.a: Because saying it sincerely is itself the act of worship; no physical deed is required.

flashcard_questions.q: At what three life moments is the Shahadah recited?
flashcard_questions.a: At birth (whispered to the newborn), at conversion to Islam, and at death.
The ritual purification Muslims must perform before Salah to be spiritually clean before Allah.
The sincere intention that must accompany every act of Islamic worship.
A single unit of Islamic prayer, with a set sequence of positions and recitations.
The direction of the Kaaba in Mecca, towards which Muslims face when praying.

flashcard_questions.q: What is Jummah and who must attend?
flashcard_questions.a: The Friday congregational prayer, which is obligatory for adult Muslim men.

flashcard_questions.q: How does du'a differ from Salah?
flashcard_questions.a: Du'a is informal personal prayer in any language at any time; Salah is structured ritual prayer in Arabic at set times.

flashcard_questions.q: Name three acts in the Shi'a Ten Obligatory Acts not in the Sunni Five Pillars.
flashcard_questions.a: Khums, Amr-bil-Maroof and Nahi Anil Munkar (also Tawalla and Tabarra).
A Shi'a obligation to give twenty percent of certain earnings to the Imam or his representatives.

glossary_terms.definition: Submission or surrender to the will of Allah; the act of living in total obedience to God.
The intention or sincerity of purpose that must accompany every act of worship in Islam.
The five core acts of worship obligatory for every Sunni Muslim: Shahadah, Salat, Zakat, Sawm and Hajj.
The Islamic declaration of faith: 'There is no god but Allah, and Muhammad is the messenger of Allah.' The first Pillar of Sunni Islam.
The absolute oneness and indivisibility of Allah; the central concept in Islamic theology.
The ritual washing carried out before Islamic prayer, involving the face, hands, arms and feet.
The direction of the Kaaba in Mecca, towards which Muslims face when praying.
A single unit of Islamic prayer, consisting of a prescribed sequence of positions and recitations.
The Friday noon congregational prayer, which is obligatory for adult male Muslims.
The sermon delivered by the imam before the Friday congregational prayer.
Personal, informal prayer or supplication in Islam, spoken in any language at any time, distinct from the formal ritual of Salah.
